en: *Hevajrabhaṭṭārakacakraviṃśikāstotra* by Saroruhapāda.
Extant manuscripts: CTRC Box 110, pp. 37–38 (not seen); Ṅor manuscript NSUG Xc 14/39, HSS §34;
edited by Luo Hong as announced by Isaacson (2010: 123); Tibetan translation also available, see van der Kuijp (1987).
I bow down to Hevajra, the Hero, the non-duality of wisdom and means, who is the supreme nature of all phenomena, the primordial, and who abides within the self of all. 1.
With devotion, I bow to that Lord, whose neck is embraced by Nairātmyā;
whose tawny hair blazes upward; who has eight faces and three eyes on each;
and whose uppermost pair of roots [of the faces] are white and black, while those on the right and the other side are white and red. (2)
I bow down to him whose remaining faces are black.
He is endowed with eight skulls held in his eight right arms, which contain an elephant, a horse, a donkey, a cow, a camel, a man, a dog, and a buffalo.

I bow to Him who holds in the skulls situated on His eight left arms the earth, water, wind, fire, moon, sun, Yama, and the Guhyakas; He who is trampled by the four Māras and whose four feet are the directions of space.
I bow to him who is blue, dancing with the sun in the *ālīḍha* posture;
who consists of four wheels, adorned with terrifying, dripping severed heads,
and beautifully decorated with the mudrās representing the purity of the Tathāgatas.
I salute that Great Bliss (Mahāsukha), whose head is marked with a double-vajra, who has the Lord of the Family upon his crown, and who has attained supreme bliss. 8.
In the east is Gaurī, born from the syllable Gaṃ, with a dark-blue body and a red left side.
I bow to her who holds a curved knife (karttikā) in her right hand, who stands treading upon Brahmā. 9.
I bow to Caurī, born from the syllable Caṃ, who is deep red in hue, holding a boar and a *ḍamaru* drum in her hands, and mounted upon Indra. 10.
I bow to Vettālī, born from the syllable *vaṃ*, who is yellow in color, resides with Upendra,
holds a bowl in her left hand and a tortoise in her right.
[I bow to] Ghasmarī at the northern gate, who is dark green and arises from the syllable *ghaṃ*.
I bow to her who is mounted upon Rudra, her hands busily occupied with a skull, a snake, and a corpse. I bow to the blue Pukkasī, born from the male [principle], who stands upon Yama,
holding an axe in her right hand and a lion in her left, possessing a terrifying form in the northeast.

I bow to Śavarī, born from the syllable Śaṃ, white in color, situated in the southeast where Kubera resides; she holds a water-pot in her left hand and a mendicant’s staff in her right. I bow to Caṇḍālī, dark as the sky, born from the syllable Caṃ, located in the southwest.
I bow to the right wheel, the crusher of Rākṣasas;
I salute the Ḍombī born from the syllable "Ḍaṃ," who dwells in the northwest and resides in Vemacitrin, holding a threatening gesture and a vajra in her hands, and possessing a variegated luster.
Standing in the *ardhaparyaṅka* dance posture, adorned with the five mudrās,
all of them naked and three-eyed— I bow down to them all with devotion.
Purified as the aggregates and elements, they arise from the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*).
I bow with my whole being to all these who bestow happiness;
I always bow correctly to all those who delight in great bliss, having emerged from the seed-syllables and emblems attached to their own right arms.
The Lord, who was born from the pair of seed-syllables situated within the cavity of the moon and sun, together with his consort,
having by means of skillful means fashioned this triple world in the form of his own mandala,
has withdrawn all of it— along with the wisdom that bestows true bliss— into himself.
Homage to him who is dissolved in his own state, the nectar-essence of the passion of wisdom!
(20) Having praised Hevajra, the lord of the circle of ḍākinīs and the gods, by whatever merit I have acquired, may the world become equal to that! (21)
The *Cakraviṃśikā-stotra* (Twenty-Verse Praise) of the venerable Lord Hevajra is completed.
This is the work of the accomplished master Siddhācārya Saroruhapāda. ||o||
